      <content name="title"><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Viral <span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions.</p><p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> can be an acute (short-term) infection or a <span class="qt0">chronic</span> (long-term) infection. Some types of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> cause only acute infections. Other types can cause both acute and <span class="qt0">chronic</span> infections.</p>What causes <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p>There are different types of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>, with different causes:</p><ul><li>Viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> is the most common type. It is caused by one of several viruses -- <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> viruses A, B, C, D, and E. In the United States, A, B, and C are the most common.</li><li>Alcoholic <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> is caused by heavy alcohol use</li><li>Toxic <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> can be caused by certain poisons, chemicals, medicines, or supplements</li><li>Autoimmune <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> is a <span class="qt0">chronic</span> type in which your body's immune system attacks your liver. The cause is not known, but genetics and your environment may play a role.</li></ul>How is viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> spread?<p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis A and hepatitis</span> E usually spread through contact with food or water that was contaminated with an infected person's stool. You can also get <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> E by eating undercooked pork, deer, or shellfish.</p><p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> B, <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> C, and <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">hepatitis</span></span><span class="qt3"> D</span> spread through contact with the blood of someone who has the disease. <span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> B and D may also spread through contact with other body fluids. This can happen in many ways, such as sharing drug needles or having unprotected sex.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p>The risks are different for the different types of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>. For example, with most of the viral types, your risk is higher if you have unprotected sex.  People who drink a lot over long periods of time are at risk for alcoholic <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p>Some people with <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> do not have symptoms and do not know they are infected. If you do have symptoms, they may include:</p><ul><li>Fever</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Dark urine</li><li>Clay-colored bowel movements</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Jaundice, yellowing of your skin and eyes</li></ul><p>If you have an acute infection, your symptoms can start anywhere between 2 weeks to 6 months after you got infected. If you have a <span class="qt0">chronic</span> infection, you may not have symptoms until many years later.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> cause?<p><span class="qt0">Chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> can lead to complications such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver failure, and liver cancer. Early diagnosis and treatment of <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> may prevent these complications.</p>How is <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms and medical history</li><li>Will do a physical exam</li><li>Will likely do blood tests, including tests for viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span></li><li>Might do imaging tests, such as an ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI</li><li>May need to do a liver biopsy to get a clear diagnosis and check for liver damage</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> depends on which type you have and whether it is acute or <span class="qt0">chronic</span>. Acute viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> often goes away on its own. To feel better, you may just need to rest and get enough fluids. But in some cases, it may be more serious. You might even need treatment in a hospital.</p><p>There are different medicines to treat the different <span class="qt0">chronic</span> types of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>. Possible other treatments may include surgery and other medical procedures. People who have alcoholic <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> need to stop drinking. If your <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> leads to liver failure or liver cancer, you may need a liver transplant.</p>Can <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> be prevented?<p>There are different ways to prevent or lower your risk for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>, depending on the type of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>. For example, not drinking too much alcohol can prevent alcoholic <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>. There are vaccines to prevent <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> A and B. Autoimmune <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> cannot be prevented.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hepatitisb.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> B</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HBV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions.</p>What is <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> B is a type of viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span>. It can cause an acute (short-term) or <span class="qt0">chronic</span> (long-term) infection. People with an acute infection usually get better on their own without treatment. Some people with <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B will need treatment.</p><p>Thanks to a vaccine, <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B is not very common in the United States. It is more common in certain parts of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.</p>What causes <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt2">Hepatitis</span> B is caused by the <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B virus. The virus spreads through contact with blood, semen, or other body fluids from a person who has the virus.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, but the risk is higher in:</p><ul><li>Infants born to mothers who have <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B</li><li>People who inject drugs or share needles, syringes, and other types of drug equipment</li><li>Sex partners of people with <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they are not using latex or polyurethane condoms during sex</li><li>Men who have sex with men</li><li>People who live with someone who has <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they use the same razor, toothbrush, or nail clippers</li><li>Health care and public-safety workers who are exposed to blood on the job</li><li>Hemodialysis patients</li><li>People who have lived in or traveled often to parts of the world where <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B is common</li><li>People who have diabetes, <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> C, or HIV</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Often, people with <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B don't have symptoms. Adults and children over 5 are more likely to have symptoms than younger children.</p><p>Some people with acute <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B have symptoms 2 to 5 months after infection. These symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Yellowish eyes and skin, called jaundice</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, you may not have symptoms until complications develop. This could be decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B screening is important, even if you have no symptoms. Screening means that you are tested for a disease even though you don't have symptoms. If you are at high risk, your health care provider may suggest  screening.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B cause?<p>In rare cases, acute <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B can cause liver failure.</p><p><span class="qt0">Chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B can develop into a serious disease that causes long-term health problems such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and liver failure.</p><p>If you have ever had <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, the virus may become active again, or reactivated, later in life. This could start to damage the liver and cause symptoms.</p>How is <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A physical exam</li><li>Blood tests, including tests for viral <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span></li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B?<p>If you have acute <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B, you probably don't need treatment. Some people with <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B don't need treatment. But if you have a <span class="qt0">chronic</span> infection and blood tests show that <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B could be damaging your liver, you may need to take antiviral medicines.</p>Can <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B is to get the <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B vaccine.</p><p>You can also reduce your chance of <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools</li><li>Not sharing personal items, such as toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>If you think you have been in contact with the <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B virus, see your health care provider right away. Your provider may give you a dose of the <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B vaccine to prevent infection. In some cases, your provider may also give you a medicine called <span class="qt2">hepatitis</span> B immune globulin (HBIG). You need to get the vaccine and the HBIG (if needed) as soon as possible after coming into contact with the virus. It is best if you can get them within 24 hours.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
